title: AI made feasibility almost trivial. It has not touched value, viability, or usability.
author: Benedikt Kantus
summary: This Leading in Product essay answers the idea that AI-assisted coding makes product managers an expensive layer of overhead. The author argues that customers buy solutions to problems, not software, so a product is far more than its code. He walks through what product teams actually own: the moat, positioning, pricing, messaging, go-to-market strategy and the business case. Using the four product risks of value, viability, usability and feasibility, he says AI has made feasibility almost trivial but has not touched the other three. When shipping is easy the bottleneck moves from execution to judgment, and being wrong becomes faster and cheaper to do. He advises founders and product leaders to stop asking whether they need product managers and ask whether their product managers are focused on customer problems, positioning and the business case rather than tickets and standups.
points: Customers buy solutions to problems rather than software, so treating the product as only its code is the founder's most common mistake.
When anyone can build an app in an afternoon, the moat shifts to customer insight, brand trust, proprietary data and integrations.
Pricing, positioning and messaging are strategic decisions that decide whether a good product wins or quietly fails.
Of the four product risks, AI has made feasibility almost trivial while value, viability and usability remain as hard as before.
Leaders should audit whether product managers are working on customer problems and the business case, since PMs who mostly write tickets are a focus problem, not a headcount problem.
quotes: Because that person was never just managing the code. They were managing everything else.
But customers do not buy software. They buy solutions to problems.
In a world where anyone can spin up a working app in an afternoon, technical execution is no longer a differentiator.
Price too low, and you attract customers who drain your support team and leave the moment someone cheaper shows up.
AI has made feasibility almost trivial. It has not touched the other three. Not even close.
When anyone can ship a feature in an afternoon, the scarce resource is no longer execution. It is judgment.
And they become more consequential, not less, precisely because the cost of building is now so low. You can be wrong faster than ever before.
The teams that win in an AI-accelerated world will not be the ones who ship the fastest. They will be the ones who decide the best.
